parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: magnetic force on a moving charge
Fleming's left-hand rule for negative charge
hints: Hint 1: Think about what two things must be present for a magnetic force on a charge. Check the angle between the electron velocity as it enters and the magnetic field direction.
Hint 2: For direction, remember current is opposite to electron flow. Try Fleming's left-hand rule for a positive current first, then reverse the force direction for electrons.
parts.proper_answer: Magnitude $= Bqv$. Direction is $P \to Q$ (or $E \to F$, or $S \to R$, or $H \to G$), i.e. sideways across the slice, perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Magnitude from $F = BQv \sin\theta$**
You have a charge of magnitude $q$ moving at speed $v$ at $90^{\circ}$ to field $B$. For motion perpendicular to the field, $\sin\theta = 1$, so the magnetic force magnitude is simply $$F = Bqv$$ The minus sign on $-q$ only tells you the charge is negative, it does not change the size of the force.

Step 2: **Direction using Fleming's left-hand rule**
Point your First finger down for $B$ and your second finger for conventional current. Conventional current is opposite to electron motion, so it points out of the slice toward the incoming electrons. Your thumb then points one way for positive charge. Because electrons are negative, the real force is opposite to this. That gives a force sideways across the slice, along $P \to Q$ or $E \to F$. In other words the electrons are pushed toward one side face of the slice.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Follow where the electrons from (a) are pushed. They will pile up on one side face, leaving the opposite side positive, so the Hall voltage must appear between that pair of opposite faces.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where charge builds up**
The magnetic force in (a) pushes all the moving electrons toward one long side face. That face becomes negative and the opposite long side face is left positive. The separation of charge sets up the Hall voltage $V_H$ between those two opposite side faces, which are EHSP and FGRQ. It is not between the entrance and exit faces, and not between top and bottom.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: In $V_H = BI/ntq$, $t$ is the size of the slice measured along the direction of $B$. Look at Fig. 8.1 and see which edge is parallel to the $B$ arrows.
parts.proper_answer: $t$ is PE (or QF or RG or SH), the vertical edge parallel to $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Meaning of $t$ in the Hall formula**
$B$ is directed vertically down into face PQRS. The thickness $t$ is always the dimension parallel to $B$, i.e. the distance between the top face PQRS and the bottom face EFGH. On the diagram that vertical edge is labelled PE, and equivalently QF, SH or RG.

parts.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: density, molar mass and Avogadro constant
unit conversion from cm-3 to m-3
hints: Hint 1: Start from density $2.7\text{ g cm}^{-3}$ and molar mass $27\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. How many moles are in $1\text{ cm}^3$, and how many atoms does that correspond to if one mole has $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms?
Hint 2: Remember one free electron per atom, and convert the final answer from per $\text{cm}^3$ to per $\text{m}^3$ by multiplying by $10^6$.
parts.proper_answer: $n \approx 6.0 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}$ e.g. moles per $\text{cm}^3 = 2.7/27 = 0.10$, atoms per $\text{m}^3 = 0.10 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \times 10^6 = 6.0 \times 10^{28}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From mass density to atoms per volume**
Aluminium has nucleon number 27, so one mole has mass $27\text{ g}$. In $1\text{ cm}^3$ the mass is $2.7\text{ g}$, so $$\text{amount} = \frac{2.7}{27} = 0.10\text{ mol}$$ One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms, so $1\text{ cm}^3$ contains $$0.10 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 6.02 \times 10^{22}\text{ atoms}$$

Step 2: **Convert to per cubic metre**
There is one free electron per atom, so this is also the number of carriers per $\text{cm}^3$. Since $1\text{ m}^3 = 10^6\text{ cm}^3$: $$n = 6.02 \times 10^{22} \times 10^6 \approx 6.0 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}$$ Equivalently, using atomic mass $27 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and density $2.7 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$: $$n = \frac{2.7 \times 10^3}{27 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 6.0 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Identify each symbol in $V_H = BI/ntq$: $B = 0.15\text{ T}$, $I = 4.6\text{ A}$, $n$ from (i), and $q$ is the elementary charge.
Hint 2: Convert the thickness to metres before substituting: $t = 0.090\text{ mm} = 0.090 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$, then evaluate $BI$ divided by $ntq$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set up the Hall equation in SI units**
Use $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ with $B = 0.15\text{ T}$, $I = 4.6\text{ A}$, $n = 6.0 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}$, $t = 0.090 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ and $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.

Step 2: **Calculate the tiny Hall voltage**
$$V_H = \frac{0.15 \times 4.6}{6.0 \times 10^{28} \times 0.090 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$V_H \approx 8.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ V}$$ This very small voltage is typical for a metal because $n$ is so large.
